## Overview

The Tobelo people, also called *O'Hoberera Manyawa* in Tobelo, are one of the northern Halmahera peoples of eastern Indonesia. They live mainly in the northern part of the Maluku Islands and on the eastern side of North Halmahera Regency. The Tobelo-speaking heartland lies in the six administrative districts of Tobelo, on the western shore of Kao Bay, in the central part of Halmahera Utara Regency. The district capital, also called Tobelo, is a regional commercial and administrative center and the largest settlement on Halmahera. The total Tobelo population is about 85,000. They speak Indonesian, Ternate, and Tobelo, a North Halmahera language with several dialects. Their folk culture includes coastal settlement, bamboo houses, fishing, farming, sago production, songs, dance, and wedding ceremonies.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

**Tapa cloth** — Earlier Tobelo clothing used tapa cloth garments, but these were replaced by common clothes and European-style clothing.

**Motif vocabulary.** The sources name no Tobelo textile motifs.

### Clothing & dress

Earlier, the Tobelo wore tapa cloth garments. These were later replaced by common clothing and clothing of European style. The sources do not distinguish documented men's and women's garments, head coverings, belts, footwear, or other named dress types. In wedding proceedings, women display “women’s wealth,” and their participation includes dancing with a bushcraft knife in the hand. The available material does not identify this as a named garment or adornment tradition.

### Architecture

Tobelo settlements are mainly located along the coastline, although the people are described as highly mobile. Their ground skeleton-stilted houses are called *tathu*. These houses are built from bamboo, with roofing made from sago-palm leaves or roof shingles. The sources also describe forest Tobelo, or Inner Tobelo, living in the depths of Halmahera near river valleys. Some Togutil people later settled in houses built by regional authorities as part of social integration programs, including in Dodaga (Maba).

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

They mention bamboo house construction, a bushcraft knife used by women during wedding proceedings, and a special refined wedding table made in the form of a canoe.

### Jewelry & body adornment

They describe women displaying “women’s wealth” during wedding proceedings.

## Music & performance

Song and dance are described as the most common forms of Tobelo folk art. Traditional songs are performed during the celebration of a marriage, together with feasting and dancing. A wedding documentary, “Tobelo Marriage,” directed by Dirk Niland, was filmed in Leiden in the Netherlands in 1982 and presents the marriage ceremony and social life of the remote island society. The sources also mention a program on Indonesian national television about the habits and customs of the Togutil people, as well as a Tik Tok account publishing videos about them. No other documented performance repertoire is provided.

## Dance & theatre

Dance is one of the most common forms of Tobelo folk art. Wedding celebrations include dancing and the performance of traditional songs. During the wedding proceedings, women dance with a bushcraft knife in the hand, a performance described as indicating the importance of women in the proceedings.

## Festivals & rituals

They do describe wedding ritual and a reconciliation ceremony connected with the religious-ethnic violence of 1999–2001. In April 2001, a peaceful ceremony was held after the conflict between Muslims and Christians. The ceremony consisted of the *adat* ritual, described as customary law, together with a vow that Muslims and Christians would respect one another’s rights and renounce violence. It symbolized a decision in North Maluku to recognize adat as a guarantor of social unity and harmony.

Marriage is patrilocal, and bilateral kinship is described as inherent among the Tobelo. The size of the marriage dowry is linked to the comparative annual incomes of the households involved and to financial claims made to the groom’s side. Women’s work in preparing the wedding feast includes weaving and preparing a “rice slide” festive dish and a special refined table shaped like a canoe. In cases of incest, a special ceremony of rupturing the hereditary line is held; the sources state that sending the couple floating or drowning into the river is believed to prevent floods.

## Foodways

The main Tobelo food products are raw, dried, and salted fish, together with vegetable-based foods. These include baked and cooked products made from rice, bananas, sago, sweet potato, and cassava. Rice dishes are not common, but they are prepared on holidays. The sources describe fishing and fishery as major occupations and also mention manual farming of bananas, copra, palm wine, root crops, tubers, beans, and dry rice. Sago production is especially associated with Kao and Boeng speakers.

In the early 1980s, the forest Tobelo were described as hunting, stealing, and growing sago. They also used small fields to grow bananas, cassava, fruits, and coconuts through slash-and-burn agriculture.

## Oral tradition & literature

They mention traditional songs performed during wedding celebrations and the Tobelo-language work *O Tobelohoka manga totoade: verhalen en vertellingen in de Tobeloreesche taal*, published by Anton Hueting in 1908. The sources also identify a Tobelo Bible App and describe audiovisual and social-media presentations of Togutil habits and customs. No contemporary literary revival or formal preservation project is otherwise described.

## Language & religion

Tobelo is a North Halmahera language spoken on Halmahera and parts of neighboring islands. Its principal dialects are Heleworuru, Boeng, Dodinga, Lake Paca, Kukumutuk, and Popon. The last three are also known as Tugutil. The sources additionally discuss Galela, Loloda, Modole, Pagu, and Tabaru as related North Halmaheran varieties, although most speakers consider them distinct languages from Tobelo.

Among the Tobelo, Indonesian, Ternate, and Tobelo are spoken. The majority are Reformed Christians, while others are Sunni Muslims. Traditional beliefs, including vestiges of shamanism and the cult of spirits, continue to influence everyday life. Forest Tobelo began professing the Bible in the late 1980s after decades of resistance. Their Christianity came through American missionaries rather than through the Tobelo language-speaking societies with which they maintain family and marriage ties.
